groups.title: Professional services
groups.scenario: A client asks for advice or a deliverable. The value is keeping the brief, agreed fee, work, approval and invoice together.

groups.title: IT and managed services
groups.scenario: A client needs technology supplied, installed or supported. Keep the request, price, engineer, device, supplier and resolution connected.

groups.title: Manufacturing and production
groups.scenario: An order depends on materials, production capacity, inspection, dispatch and payment. Preserve the chain from promise to delivered goods.

groups.title: Retail, wholesale and distribution
groups.scenario: A customer buys or orders something. Stock, suppliers, fulfilment and the resulting money must agree.

groups.title: Construction and contracting
groups.scenario: An accepted job has scope, people, materials, variations and claims. Keep those decisions together as the site changes.

groups.title: Healthcare and wellness administration
groups.scenario: A service enquiry becomes an appointment, a resource commitment and a financial record. Keep non-clinical administration dependable.

groups.title: Mining and industrial services
groups.scenario: A site obligation needs an agreed scope, access, people, equipment and completion evidence before billing.

groups.title: Property and real estate
groups.scenario: A buyer, seller, tenant or landlord makes a request. Each viewing, follow-up, service job and financial decision needs an owner.

groups.title: Education, training and skills
groups.scenario: A learning commitment is a promise about dates, trainers, people, materials and results. Run that operational programme coherently.

groups.title: Marketing, media and creative work
groups.scenario: A client brief becomes scoped creative work, reviews, sign-off and an agreed fee. Keep feedback and deadlines from drifting.

groups.title: Logistics and field services
groups.scenario: A delivery or field request needs a slot, the right person, proof of completion and the right invoice.

groups.title: Hospitality, food and accommodation
groups.scenario: A booking or order is a promise to deliver a dependable experience. Connect reservations, people, stock, suppliers and money.

groups.title: Agriculture, farming and agribusiness
groups.scenario: A seasonal plan depends on people, equipment, inputs, harvesting or service delivery and payment.

groups.title: Repairs, installations and maintenance
groups.scenario: A broken asset or new installation starts with a request and ends when the customer has evidence of completion and knows what to pay.

groups.title: One-person and independent businesses
groups.scenario: One person is responsible for finding the client, doing the job and getting paid. The working day should feel manageable.

groups.title: Nonprofits and community organisations
groups.scenario: A programme promise must be matched by people, spending, completed work and an honest account to those supporting it.

groups.title: Leadership, management and enterprise
groups.scenario: A leader wants to understand commitments, execution, accountability and money without rebuilding the truth each Friday.

gardener.title: A gardener should finish the day knowing tomorrow’s jobs and which clients still need an invoice.
gardener.story: You receive a WhatsApp message while cutting a lawn. Another customer wants a once-off clean-up. You need a quote, a date, enough help, and a reminder to bill. That should not require five systems or a late-night memory test.
steps: Keep the customer, address and preferred visit pattern together
Estimate the job and capture what the customer accepted
See the day’s route and the work still to be done
Record completion, travel or materials in the same job history
Follow the invoice and set the next repeat visit

estate agent.title: An estate agent should never lose a viewing, a client conversation or the next follow-up.
estate agent.story: A potential buyer calls after a viewing. A seller wants feedback and a landlord has a maintenance query. These are three different commitments, but each needs a responsible next step and a history you can actually find.
steps: Capture buyer, seller and landlord relationships clearly
Set the viewing or follow-up with its owner and due date
Retain the agreed correspondence and administrative actions
Connect property-related jobs to the contractor and approval trail
Review what is outstanding before the next client conversation

plumber.title: A plumber should move from the first call to a paid, properly recorded job.
plumber.story: A client sends a picture of a leaking pipe. You need to assess urgency, quote a visit, bring the right parts, document the work and invoice. The useful software is the software that follows that job through.
steps: Record the fault, property and urgency
Agree the visit and scope before promising a fixed repair price
Confirm parts, supplier needs and technician availability
Document the work and any follow-up the customer accepted
Invoice against the completed visit and track the payment

property manager.title: A property manager should see every open obligation across landlords, tenants and contractors.
property manager.story: A tenant reports a broken gate, a landlord approves a quote and the contractor says the repair is finished. The missing piece is often not effort; it is the complete, reliable history of the job.
steps: Capture the request and the affected property
Assign responsibility and confirm owner or landlord approvals
Compare supplier quotes and schedule the contractor
Record completion evidence and any tenant follow-up
Reconcile the cost and outstanding administration

ceo.title: A chief executive should see business priorities and their financial consequences without chasing five reports.
ceo.story: Sales look healthy, but open jobs, supplier commitments and outstanding receipts tell the more important story. Leadership needs decisions backed by connected source records.
steps: Agree the operating priorities and the measures that matter
Make commitments and delegated authority visible
Track execution across sales, work, purchasing and people
Review receivables, obligations, exceptions and current cash exposure
Follow each decision back to the actual record and responsible owner

qse business owner.title: A growing QSE owner needs enterprise discipline without enterprise-level complexity.
qse business owner.story: You have passed the stage where the owner can remember every quote, supplier and customer payment. Your challenge is to delegate and keep control, while retaining the everyday simplicity the team needs.
steps: Turn the accepted quote into a clear operating commitment
Give teams ownership and approval boundaries
Connect procurement, stock and staff assignments to work
Monitor the cash consequences and unresolved exceptions
Review growth decisions using traceable business evidence

accountant.title: An accountant needs financial clarity tied to the work that created each transaction.
accountant.story: A client asks why a payment is unmatched. Another asks which job drove the invoice. Rather than reconstructing a trail, you should see the originating commercial and operational record.
steps: Identify the client, period and underlying source transactions
Review invoices, receipts, allocations and exceptions
Investigate mismatches against approved business records
Provide a transparent position without duplicating spreadsheets

spaza shop owner.title: A spaza shop owner should know what sold, what to buy and what money is available.
spaza shop owner.story: Stock sells quickly, some customers buy on account and a supplier arrives with new prices. Simple records should make the next purchase and the end-of-day picture easier, not harder.
steps: Track key items and the prices you sell at
Know the stock that needs replenishment
Record supplier purchases and the amounts still owed
Understand sales, customer balances and daily cash
Make the next buying decision from current information

stages.label: Working for myself
stages.heading: Keep the day simple
stages.story: Find your next customer action, the work you promised and the invoices you still need to send. You do not need a department or technical vocabulary to follow a business journey.

stages.label: Microbusiness / EME
stages.heading: Bring the first team together
stages.story: As jobs and customer conversations grow, the business needs one understandable picture and basic handoffs. EME is a separate B-BBEE classification, subject to the applicable code.

stages.label: Small or growing SME
stages.heading: Stay in control as work grows
stages.story: Connect customer demand, quotations, fulfilment, expenses and staff responsibility without creating disconnected islands of software.

stages.label: QSE (B-BBEE category)
stages.heading: Add discipline without losing agility
stages.story: A Qualifying Small Enterprise commonly sits between R10 million and R50 million annual turnover under the generic B-BBEE Codes, but sector-code thresholds can differ. QSE is a B-BBEE classification, not a separate technology feature or universal business-size label.

stages.label: Medium-sized business
stages.heading: Connect functions and managers
stages.story: Organise approvals, departments, shared resources, purchasing and financial decisions in one operating context. National enterprise-size thresholds vary by sector.

stages.label: Large / enterprise organisation
stages.heading: Make authority and evidence visible
stages.story: Coordinate multiple departments and sites with role-based access, governance, traceability and controlled deployment scope. Enterprise suitability remains subject to qualification.
